ff40aa391079.title: What ingesting these documents cost
ff40aa391079.content: Every rule below was learned by getting it wrong here first. They live in who-iris/skills/iris-dspace.md — read the skill — and this page is generated from that file, so the two cannot drift. There are 22 of them, against 222 item(s) in the catalogue, 12 of which this repository actually holds the bytes for. Why a page and not just a skill. A skill is read by an agent about to act. A reader deciding whether to trust what was ingested needs the same facts and will not open a skill file to get them. Same text, two audiences, one source — the skill. Requirements a record can be checked against # Requirement Why, in one line R1 Resolve by Handle where one exists; treat UUID and govdoc as secondary only the Handle is guaranteed outside WHO R2 Never deduplicate dc.identifier.uri the second one is evidence of a host that vanished R3 Preserve repetition on every field, not a known list four fields repeat in a single record; assume more do R4 Treat an absent language as unasserted , never as en both states occur in one record R5 Carry dc.subject.mesh as a controlled value with its authority it can be resolved and subsumed; a keyword cannot R6 Model bitstreams per bundle , with size and format on the bitstream an item is not a file R7 Model containment as a list of paths four levels deep, and multiple mappings are legal R8 Never infer metadata from the PDF when a record exists OCR off a title page catalogued the WHO Editorial Style Manual as Abies R9 Record what the source says even when it contradicts the file dc.description says 30 p. ; the PDF has 33 R10 An item with no known collection carries parents: [] — never a guessed one held-and-unplaceable is a STATE; inventing containment is unfalsifiable R11 Key a node by path when its UUID is not in the capture an invented UUID resolves to nothing while looking authoritative R12 Keep the page captured and the identifier apart /items/<uuid>/full is what was fetched; the Handle is what the item IS R13 A materialized claim must name bytes that EXIST, and something must check it an unchecked claim can name no bytes and still pass as held R14 Read a storage figure in the units that round-trip its own bytes IRIS prints "GB" for what its byte counts make GiB — a 7% error R15 Never fall back to a parent URL when an item has no upstream URI "no upstream URI recorded" is the answer; the front page is a lie that resolves R16 A partial transcription must SAY it is partial a truncated abstract that does not declare itself cannot be told from a short one R17 Hold what you hold: model the bitstreams whose bytes are here the handbook lists 8 upstream; this repository has 1 R18 Do not "correct" a record that looks wrong the English-titled editorial manual really does carry an Italian ISBN R19 A derived figure must round-trip the figure it was derived from round(361.55 × 1024³) bytes must render back as 361.55 GiB R20 An item count and a file count are different denominators 273,559 against 1,057,223 — a fraction built from the wrong one is off by 3.86× R21 Mint stable URIs at the extractor (Upstream Skolemization) minting https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} at extraction leaves no blank nodes for a later pass to resolve R22 Append-only streaming partition writes A 300,000 item corpus cannot accumulate uncompressed in working memory; write quads directly to partition file streams Settled 2026-09-21 — bean yl5w Every ORIGINAL localPath in this catalogue named who-iris/uploads/ while the bytes sat in cat-harness/uploads/ , and check:catalogue did not look at localPath at all — so three materialized claims resolved to nothing while the gate printed clean . The three sources now sit beside their own intake records at who-iris/uploads/<slug>/ , the page generator's fallback is deleted, and check:catalogue verifies every localPath — with could not determine as its own answer, because an unreadable file is not a missing one. iris.who.int is egress-blocked from the environment that generates this page, so nothing here was fetched from IRIS. Every record was transcribed from a capture the owner supplied. Where a transcription is partial, the record says so.

045b18546490.title: IRIS CDN Exporter: deployment
045b18546490.content: Where the IRIS CDN Exporter processes run, where they write, and where the secrets live. The short version: GitHub Actions runs the exporter. Cloudflare holds and serves everything it exports. GitHub Pages only previews. The pieces Piece Service Holds Runner GitHub Actions in litlfred/who-iris ( .github/workflows/iris-cdn.yml ) nothing between runs; each run's report goes to the workflow log Release history git repository on Cloudflare Artifacts BagIt tag files, tagmanifest-sha256.txt.jws , and state/*.json (cursor, initial-load checkpoint, sizes, md5, uuids, metadata hashes, withdrawals) Bytes Cloudflare R2 bucket PDFs, item records, item manifests and their JWSs, graph partitions ( .nq.gz ), each under sha256/<aa>/<digest> CDN Cloudflare, in front of R2 on a custom domain cached copies only, with an immutable cache policy DID document served from the CDN domain did.json with the public key(s), a did:web document Signing key GitHub environment secret the P-256 private JWK Previews GitHub Pages of litlfred/who-iris and WHO/who-iris the site, reading exported data from the CDN; three materialized items for testing Cloudflare: what to set up Workers Paid plan , $5 a month. Artifacts needs it, and it is in open beta. ( changelog ) Artifacts namespace and repository. Create the namespace in the dashboard. Then create the repository: npx wrangler artifacts repos create who-iris-releases --namespace <ns> . The remote is https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.artifacts.cloudflare.net/git/<ns>/who-iris-releases.git . A repository created now is capped at 1 GB ( limits ). That is why git holds only the release history, and the bytes go to R2. R2 bucket , for example who-iris-cdn . Storage is about $0.015 per GB-month and egress is free, so ~361 GiB costs about $5.40 a month. Custom domain on the bucket, which puts the Cloudflare CDN in front of it. Then add a Cache Rule with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for sha256/* . Content-addressed objects never change, so they can be cached forever. API token with permissions for Artifacts (edit) and the R2 bucket (object read and write). Scope it to this one account. GitHub: where each secret goes In litlfred/who-iris , go to Settings → Environments → New environment and name it iris-cdn-release . Deployment branches: main only. A job on any other branch cannot read these secrets. Required reviewers: none, so the scheduled runs stay unattended. Name Kind Where What IRIS_CDN_SIGNING_JWK secret environment iris-cdn-release the P-256 private JWK: {"kty":"EC","crv":"P-256","x":…,"y":…,"d":…} CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN secret environment iris-cdn-release the API token from step 5 R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID , R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY secret environment iris-cdn-release R2's S3-compatible credentials, for uploads IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK variable repository WHO's signing-DID public key (JWK), so verification checks the x5c chain. Verification refuses to run without it IRIS_CDN_DID variable repository the DID that publishes the signing key, e.g. did:web:<cdn-domain> IRIS_CDN_KEY_ID variable repository the key's fragment in that DID document (default release-1 ) CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID variable repository not secret IRIS_CDN_ARTIFACTS_NAMESPACE , IRIS_CDN_ARTIFACTS_REPO variable repository the Artifacts namespace and repository from step 2 IRIS_CDN_R2_BUCKET variable repository the bucket from step 3 IRIS_CDN_ENABLED variable repository true turns the workflow on (on main only); anything else leaves it off The workflow never stores the Artifacts git token. Each run mints a write token that lasts an hour ( wrangler artifacts repos issue-token … --ttl 3600 ) and passes it to git as a Bearer header. It never goes in the remote URL. How the signing key was created and published is outside this deployment; see key custody . What runs when Workflow trigger Process Environment schedule: 0 2 * * * nightly change ingest iris-cdn-release schedule: 0 4 * * 0 weekly reconciliation (Sunday) iris-cdn-release workflow_dispatch with mode: nightly or reconcile the same, on demand iris-cdn-release Runs never overlap (one concurrency group), and a job times out after 350 minutes. Each run clones the release history, runs bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts <mode> --release release , commits and pushes only if something changed, then verifies the published release. The initial load is not a workflow mode. It is run by hand: bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts initial-load --release <checkout> --budget <json-or-file> . The budget's maxBatchesPerRun bounds one run, and the next run resumes from the checkpoint in state/initial-load.json ; the caller commits and pushes the checkout after each run. Previews on GitHub Pages The who-iris site on GitHub Pages renders pages from data it reads from the CDN . It never copies the export into the Pages artifact. The three items materialized today stay in this repository as test fixtures. That keeps Pages small, and a preview always shows what the CDN actually serves. Still open The domain. The DID is tied to the domain, so this has to be settled before the first signed release. The recommendation is a domain the owner adds to Cloudflare.

c071c309a496.title: IRIS CDN Exporter: processes
c071c309a496.content: How WHO IRIS gets from its DSpace server to a signed, versioned copy on Cloudflare: one initial load, then a nightly change ingest, a weekly reconciliation, and one signed release per run. The diagrams below are rendered from the BPMN files in processes/ . The BPMN files are the source of truth, and each step names the skill that carries it out. Where the infrastructure runs, where it writes and where the secrets live is in deployment ; how releases and items are signed is in iris-cdn-signing ; the no-churn rule every step obeys is in iris-cdn-exporter . Actors Lane Who or what Owner Approves scope, budget and the storage target IRIS CDN Exporter (agent) Plans and reviews, and opens beans for anomalies. Never holds the key, and never pushes to a WHO repository Build pipeline The scripts in scripts/iris-cdn/ , run by GitHub Actions. Same input, same bytes Release signer Holds the P-256 private key and signs what changed Cloudflare git (Artifacts) A git repository on Cloudflare holding the release history: BagIt tag files, the release signature, and state files (cursor, checkpoint) Cloudflare R2 + CDN Every byte named by its SHA-256 and served with an immutable cache. Also serves did.json Verifier Anyone. Resolves the key from the DID document, never from the package 1. Initial load processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn . The load covers metadata and the PDFs. It refuses to start without a budget stating the upstream totals and a request rate ( run.ts initial-load --budget <json-or-file> ). It runs in batches of one page of one collection (100 items by default) and checkpoints after every batch in state/initial-load.json , so a stopped load resumes where it left off. Bytes that fail the IRIS checksum are quarantined, not published. 2. Nightly change ingest processes/iris-cdn-nightly.bpmn . The pipeline lists the items IRIS changed since the cursor, using the DSpace REST API only, fetches only those, and rebuilds the graph in full. If nothing changed, it publishes nothing and makes no commit. The cursor moves forward only after the release verifies. 3. Weekly reconciliation processes/iris-cdn-reconcile.bpmn . REST does not report deletions, so once a week every item ID is compared with what the library holds. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Withdrawn items are marked as withdrawn and their bytes stay addressable. 4. Sign and publish (called by all three) processes/iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn . Each changed library item gets a detached JWS over its own manifest, and the release is a BagIt bag whose signed tag manifest pins every item manifest and signature (see iris-cdn-signing ). Payload objects go to R2 first. The tag files and the signature are committed to Cloudflare git last, in one commit. A release that does not verify must be reverted so the previous release stays served: run.ts verify reverts the commit in its checkout, but in the workflow that revert is not pushed, so for now it is a manual git revert in the release repository. The signing key already exists and is published outside these processes; see key custody . When metadata changes and the PDF does not A record and its files are stored and diffed separately. A Dublin Core edit produces a new record, and therefore a new digest, while the PDF keeps its digest and is not fetched again. Renamed communities and collections are caught by re-reading them nightly. Edits that do not move lastModified are caught by the weekly metadata hash check. See the skill iris-rest-feed . Skills and code Skill What it covers iris-cdn-exporter The agent role and the no-churn rule iris-rest-feed The DSpace REST change walk, the weekly reconciliation, fixity, the live endpoint shapes iris-cdn-signing BagIt, the detached JWS, did:web , key rotation iris-oxigraph The graph partitions the rebuild produces iris-dspace What an IRIS record holds The code is in scripts/iris-cdn/ : run.ts (the runner, with modes initial-load , nightly , reconcile , verify and revert ), bag.ts , signing.ts and rest-feed.ts . Its tests are scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts . The platform processes these call are in cat-harness: processes/kg/nquads-distribution.bpmn (graph partitions), processes/kg/named-query-execution.bpmn (prepared SPARQL) and processes/kg/kg-to-portal.bpmn (the general select, package, sign, distribute and verify pattern).

255c3aa2aadc.title: IRIS CDN Exporter: signing options
255c3aa2aadc.content: How to sign an IRIS CDN release: a detached JWS (option A) or a W3C Data Integrity proof (option C). Option A is the one used , as a detached JWS (ES256) on each library item plus one over the release; what is signed and how is in iris-cdn-signing . This page is the comparison behind that choice. The signing key is subordinate to WHO's signing DID: did:web:raw.githubusercontent.com:WorldHealthOrganization:tng-participants-prod:main:WHO:signing:DID ( did.json ) What WHO's DID document contains (read 2026-10-30) Field Value @context https://www.w3.org/ns/did/v1 , https://w3id.org/security/suites/jws-2020/v1 verificationMethod[0].type JsonWebKey2020 key publicKeyJwk , kty: EC , crv: P-256 , which means ES256 controller itself assertionMethod not present . Only verificationMethod is listed Three things follow: The curve is P-256, not Ed25519. A key that sits under WHO's should use the same curve, so one verifier library and one algorithm ( ES256 , RFC 7518) cover the whole chain. WHO's document uses the JWS-2020 vocabulary. JsonWebKey2020 and its context are a W3C Credentials Community Group report, not a W3C Recommendation. It is published, though, and WHO already uses it. Following the parent's form is the least surprising choice. The W3C Recommendation equivalent is JsonWebKey from Controlled Identifiers 1.0. No assertionMethod . A verifier checking WHO's key directly can only use verificationMethod . Our own DID document should still list assertionMethod , because that is how DID Core says a key may sign statements. Option A: detached JWS over the BagIt tag manifest The signed bytes are tagmanifest-sha256.txt (RFC 8493). The signature is a compact JWS with a detached payload (RFC 7515 Appendix F), alg: ES256 (RFC 7518), and kid set to a DID URL. Standards RFC 7515, RFC 7518, RFC 8493. All are IETF standards Fits WHO's DID Yes. JWS with a P-256 JWK is exactly what JsonWebKey2020 / jws-2020 describes Fits WHO SMART Trust / GDHCN tooling Yes. That ecosystem signs with ES256 over JOSE and COSE What it covers Every byte of the release, through the tag manifest and the payload manifest Churn One signature per release and one per changed item. An unchanged night has an identical tag manifest, so it gets no new signature. There is no timestamp in the header Tooling Everywhere: WebCrypto, jose , openssl , every language Verifier effort Fetch the DID document, run one ES256 verify, then sha256sum -c Weakness It signs files, not meaning. Re-serializing the graph, for example re-ordering N-Quads, breaks the digest even when the data is the same. Sorted output prevents that on our side Option C: W3C Data Integrity proof The signed object is a JSON document, for example a manifest written as a Verifiable Credential, carrying an embedded proof with type: DataIntegrityProof . Standards VC Data Integrity 1.0 and Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites 1.0. Both are W3C Recommendations of 15 May 2025 Cryptosuite ecdsa-jcs-2019 (JSON canonicalization) or ecdsa-rdfc-2019 (RDF canonicalization). P-256 is supported Fits WHO's DID Not directly. The ECDSA cryptosuites define only Multikey verification methods. WHO's key is a JsonWebKey2020 , so a Data Integrity verifier following the Recommendation would not accept WHO's key as it is published. WHO would need to add a Multikey form of the key What it covers A JSON document. The BagIt manifest is plain text, so it would have to be wrapped in a JSON or VC envelope, and no published schema exists for a file manifest as a VC . One would have to be invented, which conflicts with "no new schemas without approval" The RDF option ecdsa-rdfc-2019 can sign the graph itself , so the signature survives re-serialization. RDF canonicalization (RDFC-1.0) of ~12 million quads is heavy, and cost grows with blank nodes. We have none, which helps Churn One proof per release. created is optional, so it can be left out to keep bytes stable Tooling Fewer libraries, mostly the Digital Bazaar stack. Portals such as Moodle or an intranet are unlikely to have a verifier Comparison A: JWS C: Data Integrity Works with WHO's key as published today Yes No (needs Multikey ) Signs the whole release, PDFs included Yes Only through an invented wrapper New schema needed No Yes, a manifest-as-VC Survives graph re-serialization No (prevented by sorted output) Yes, with rdfc Verifier tooling Universal Specialist Churn None on unchanged nights None if created is omitted Why A A works with WHO's key as published, x5c fits JWS, and it needs no new schema. C's real advantage, a signature over meaning rather than bytes, can be added later for the graph alone : a second, optional ecdsa-rdfc-2019 proof over the spine and partitions, once WHO publishes a Multikey form of its key. Making our key subordinate to WHO's DID Core has no single "subordinate key" mechanism. The exporter's key carries an x5c certificate chain (RFC 7517 §4.7) ending at a certificate issued by WHO's signing key, so no edit to WHO's DID document is needed. The alternatives considered were: Way How What WHO must do Strength S1. A key inside WHO's DID Add our P-256 key to WHO's did.json as #iris-cdn . Releases are signed with kid = <WHO DID>#iris-cdn Edit tng-participants-prod Strongest and simplest to verify. It is WHO's own document S2. Our own DID, controlled by WHO Publish did:web:<cdn-domain> with controller: <WHO DID> , and have WHO's document point back to it, for example in alsoKnownAs or a service entry Add one back-reference A controller claim on its own is one-directional and proves nothing. The back-reference is what makes it checkable S3. An endorsement signed by WHO Our DID document holds our key. WHO's key signs, once, a JWS over our key's JWK thumbprint (RFC 7638) and our DID, published beside our did.json Sign once with WHO's key. No edit to WHO's repo Verifiable with the same JWS tooling. It needs re-signing when our key rotates The verifier's chain is: the JWS, then our key from our DID document, then its x5c certificates, ending at WHO's P-256 key, which the verifier is given as its trust anchor. GDHCN trust lists are not assumed anywhere in that chain.

ab0d29ce2fd3.doc: From this catalogue to somebody else's portal
ab0d29ce2fd3.title: From this catalogue to somebody else’s portal
ab0d29ce2fd3.content: This instance is a worked example of a general pattern: a knowledge graph reaching readers the repository never hears about. The pattern is the platform’s — the skill is kg-to-portal and the process is kg-to-portal.bpmn . What is on this page is the part only who-iris can say: which stages are actually built here, with this instance’s own numbers. Six stages in three zones. The publisher owns the canonical URL; the cache owns neither end. The dashed arrow is undetermined on purpose. The one distinction the drawing exists for A CDN is not a publication host. It is a layer in front of one. PUBLICATION_HOSTS answers what serves the rendering ; a cache answers what stands between the server and the reader . Model the cache as the host and the published URL becomes the cache’s — then the day the cache changes, every citation breaks and the old URL stays warm for as long as its TTL says. This page is served from GitHub Pages and its assets are also reachable through jsDelivr. Both are tool choices. The canonical answer is the one the catalogue records; the CDN is an accelerated route to the same bytes. Where this instance actually is # Stage Here 1 Select Everything in this catalogue is publishable, so the editorial cut has never had to refuse anything. An untested filter is not a working one. partial 2 Serialize kg-export emits the harness graph as JSON-LD; this instance’s catalogue is 235 nodes with 222 item(s). built 3 Package There is no manifest. The pages and assets are published individually, so nothing here can detect a file that was removed . not built 4 Sign Nothing on this preview site is signed. The catalogue records a sha256 per bitstream, which is a digest and not an attestation — anyone who can change the bytes can change the digest beside them. On the Cloudflare CDN export, each item and each release is signed with a detached JWS (ES256) under a did:web key whose publicKeyJwk.x5c chains to WHO’s signing DID; see below. not built 5 Distribute 11 generated page(s) and 172 cover(s) on GitHub Pages, with a jsDelivr route to the same bytes. built 6 Verify No consumer verifies anything, because there is nothing signed to verify. This is the stage that gets dropped, and it is dropped here. not built The numbers a transport decision would be made with Constraints need denominators. These are this instance’s, measured at generation time — not quoted, not remembered. items 222 here, of 273,559 upstream the completeness denominator files 1,057,223 upstream a different denominator; 3.86 files per item, so a fraction built from the wrong one is wrong by that factor bytes 31.91 MB held, of 361.55 GiB upstream the size-gate denominator, and the reason this catalogue is by reference served 11 page(s), 172 cover(s) what a publication period would actually move readers not measured traffic is bytes × requests, and nothing here counts requests. Unknown rather than assumed — an invented reader count would make every cost figure below it fiction Trust: did:web + x5c chained to WHO’s signing DID Owner decision, 2026-10-30 (superseding the earlier GDHCN trustlist sketch): the IRIS CDN export is signed with a subordinate P-256 key published as a verificationMethod of a W3C did:web DID document whose publicKeyJwk.x5c certificate chain ends at WHO’s signing DID ( did:web:raw.githubusercontent.com:WorldHealthOrganization:tng-participants-prod:main:WHO:signing:DID ). No GDHCN trust list is assumed. See IRIS CDN Exporter: signing options and IRIS CDN Exporter: processes . Package and digests (RFC 8493). Each release is a BagIt 1.0 bag ( bagit.txt , date-free bag-info.txt , sorted manifest-sha256.txt , and tagmanifest-sha256.txt ). Per-item and per-release detached JWS (RFC 7515 Appendix F, ES256). Each changed library item has its own manifest at items/<handle>/manifest-sha256.txt and detached signature manifest-sha256.txt.jws ; the release signs tagmanifest-sha256.txt as tagmanifest-sha256.txt.jws . Independent verification. A verifier resolves the signer’s did:web document from its HTTPS origin, checks that kid is listed in assertionMethod , verifies the ES256 signature, and validates the x5c certificate chain up to WHO’s signing-DID public key. Publishing a large graph: skeleton, payloads, one SQLite file per slice A corpus the size of IRIS can only be searched on the client if the client never downloads the whole graph. The platform’s answer is late materialization . The graph is published as three things: The skeleton, as JSON-LD. Each named subgraph — a directory of a declared graph — is published at /subgraph/<harness>/<path>/ as index.jsonld (pointers to its members and child subgraphs) and index.hydrated.jsonld (every member inline, with metadata only). The root has the pointer file only, so no single file is ever the whole graph. Payloads, by content address. Heavy content — a body, a PDF, a page of sections — lives at /payload/sha256/<hex> , named by the hash of its bytes, with a <hex>.json sidecar giving its media type. A node carries a payload link with sha256 and bytes , so a consumer can decide whether to fetch before it fetches. Per-slice SQLite. CI flattens one slice into a relational schema: one table per node type, one table per relation, and a contentless FTS5 index. It publishes the result as <slice>.<sha256>.sqlite3 , named by the hash of its bytes, with a <slice>.sqlite3.json manifest at a fixed path beside it that names the file. A row holds only the payload pointer, never the payload. The browser downloads the file, checks its sha256 against the manifest, imports it into the Origin Private File System, and opens it with the official SQLite WASM build. Nothing is parsed. The contract is in the kg-export skill, under “Named subgraphs”, “Payloads” and “Per-slice SQLite”. The procedure is the slice-sqlite-publish process. This page does not restate that contract’s rules; where the two differ, the skill is right. Measured: the four pilots These are the platform’s own slices, not this catalogue’s. They were measured on 2026-10-03 (bean q8ar ). The first open was measured in Chromium on loopback against a plain static server with no COOP/COEP headers, and includes the download and the sha256 check. slice file source as published first open beans 2.83 MB 4.82 MB of bean files ~190 ms todos 0.07 MB 18 KB of JSON ~110 ms library 2.48 MB 3.59 MB of JSON ~165 ms kg 3.40 MB 3.03 MB of JSON-LD (the whole-repo graph, without bodies) ~180 ms The VFS is opfs-sahpool , running in a Worker. It needs neither SharedArrayBuffer nor COOP/COEP, which GitHub Pages cannot send. Reopening from OPFS took about 85 ms, with no download. Without a Worker or OPFS, the verified bytes are opened in memory instead, and the page reports which mode it used. No who-iris slice is built, and none of these numbers is a who-iris number. Nothing here was measured against a CDN, either: cdn.jsdelivr.net is egress-blocked from the container that generates this page. The slice budget, and what to do above it As built: the budget is about 5 MB per file ( SIZE_BUDGET_BYTES ). It is reported in the manifest as overBudget and is not gated. The process says what to do over budget: try the no-body variant first, then stop and report the measurement. All four pilots are under it. Why IRIS will not fit one slice. This is arithmetic on the pilots, not a measurement. The pilots hold between 1.1 KB per node ( kg , 3,121 nodes) and 4.0 KB per row ( beans , 723 rows). At those rates, the 273,559 upstream items would make one file of roughly 298 to 1071 MB, before any per-bitstream row. That is about 60 to 214 times the budget. Recommended, not built: split by subgraph. A slice is one SliceDef , and nothing in the builder requires a slice to be a whole graph. A DSpace community or collection is already a directory-shaped subgraph, so the natural cut is one slice per community or collection. If one of those is still over budget, split it at the next level down. Do not split by row count: a slice should match a subgraph IRI a reader can name. Each split slice keeps the full contract, with its own manifest, row digest and determinism check. A small routing slice would let one search span all of IRIS. It would hold only titles, identifiers and the subgraph each item belongs to, so the client can then open the one slice that has the rows. That is the skeleton pattern again, one level up. CDN caching file as built recommended behind a CDN payload named by its sha256, so its bytes never change cache forever ( immutable ); a new body is a new URL subgraph JSON-LD a stable IRI whose content changes when the graph does short TTL; a long one serves an old skeleton whose payload links may have been removed as orphans since slice manifest <slice>.sqlite3.json at a fixed path; it names the slice file; the client fetches it with no-store short TTL or none; it is the one file that says which build is current slice file <slice>.<sha256>.sqlite3 , named by its sha256, so its bytes never change; OPFS keys its copy by the same sha256 cache forever ( immutable ); a new build is a new URL This section has been corrected twice. It first said that only the manifest needs a short TTL, because the client keys its copy by sha256. That held for the browser’s OPFS copy, not for a CDN: the slice file was then published at the same path every build, so a CDN could serve old bytes against a new manifest, the client would refuse them on the sha256 check, and search was down until the cache expired. That is now fixed (bean wixl ). The slice file is published at assets/slices/<slice>.<sha256>.sqlite3 , and the manifest’s file names it. A fresh manifest names a file no cache has seen. A stale one names an older file that still matches it. Why not under /payload/sha256/ : a payload is a node’s body, linked from that node and removed once nothing links to it. A slice file is linked from no node, so the payload tree would treat it as an orphan. It takes the payload rule that matters, immutable bytes at a hash-named address, without joining that tree. What a CDN can still hold, as built: for one manifest TTL, a stale manifest together with the older file it names, which is a consistent pair. It can also hold an older file that nothing names until that file expires, or a stale manifest whose file the origin has stopped serving. The page reports that last case as a 404 and asks for a reload. A manifest that names a file with a different sha256 is refused with a visible message, never opened. Each deploy writes only the current file. Old ones do not pile up on the host. GitHub Pages sends max-age=600 for every file and cannot be told to send anything else, so on Pages the manifest’s short TTL is ten minutes. No CDN layer has been chosen (bean l9v6 , still proposed ). Whichever one is chosen stands in front of the publication host, as above. The slice files and payloads go out through the same publish-to-CDN step as every other page (bean 7dek , Process_RenderKgToCdn ), behind the same four gates (bean xies ). The URL-layout check that xies asks for must therefore cover /payload/sha256/ and assets/slices/ too. How a client picks a slice As built: assets/slices/index.json ( folio-slice-index/v1 ) lists every slice built into the site. The one search page, slices/search.html?slice=<name> , lists them when no slice is named. Given a name, it reads everything else it needs from the search block of that slice’s manifest. The reader picks. The page checks the name against a pattern before using it in a path. Recommended for who-iris, not built: keep the reader’s choice, and make the choices follow the catalogue’s community and collection tree. A reader browsing a community opens that community’s slice, named in its index.jsonld . A reader searching all of IRIS opens the routing slice first. Several slices can be open at once, because each is its own file in the pool. What that costs on a phone has not been measured. What is deliberately not decided The ingestion method is undetermined , and the process diagram reaches a gateway with no default branch rather than naming one. A pull from the portal, a push to an object store, a git fetch, a signed tarball on a schedule — they differ in who initiates, in what must be reachable from where, and in what happens when a publication is missed. Drawing one as the obvious branch would record a decision nobody made. The store must be versioned; which store is a deployment choice. Hosted git is one satisfaction of that requirement, not the requirement. A portal showing a graph needs to be able to say which graph — an unversioned store cannot answer “what did this look like last term”, and that is the question a reading list asks every year. Nothing here was measured against a live CDN. cdn.jsdelivr.net is egress-blocked from the container that generates these pages, so every CDN figure would be quoted rather than measured. The owner confirmed one link by hand on 2026-09-20, and that is the whole of the evidence. What ingesting these documents cost — the requirements this instance paid for, generated from the skill that records them.

bca721b7aa99.title: Oxigraph Static Pipeline & Search Requirements
bca721b7aa99.content: How the IRIS catalogue is compiled into named graphs with Oxigraph , checked, published, and queried. How to build and query it is in the iris-oxigraph skill. [!IMPORTANT] Binary assets are never embedded in the graph. PDFs, image bitstreams and covers stay on the CDN. The graph holds typed entities, Dublin Core values, containment, and each bitstream's file name, media type, byte size and copyright verdict. 1. Pipeline Architecture & Placement The pipeline is modelled in the cat-harness BPMN process files, which are the source of truth: Package and distribute partitioned N-Quads (spine, community partitions, manifest, prepared queries): processes/kg/nquads-distribution.bpmn Run a prepared SPARQL query in Oxigraph (browser WASM or local engine): processes/kg/named-query-execution.bpmn How this instance feeds the pipeline from IRIS and publishes to Cloudflare is in IRIS CDN Exporter: processes ; its nightly full rebuild calls nquads-distribution . 2. Pipeline Integration Stages Stage 1: Build-Time Ingestion, Skolemization & 2-Tier Partitioning Input , either: catalogue/nodes/*.json (communities, collections, items, bitstreams) and site/dublin-core/*.dc.jsonld (Qualified Dublin Core records conforming to dublin-core.ts ); or --records <dir> : DSpace records exported by scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts . Tool: scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts ( --out <dir> , default dist/oxigraph/ ). Actions: Skolemization: mint deterministic URIs ( https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} ) for every anonymous compound Dublin Core object. The build fails if any blank node ( _: ) remains. Partitioning: Tier 1 (Spine) : <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine> — hierarchy, item Handles, title, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz . Tier 2 (Partitions) : <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}> — the full Dublin Core of each community's items (MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial tags, govdoc, ISBN). iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz . Catalogue and metadata graphs : iris_who_int_graph_catalogue.nq(.gz) and iris_who_int_graph_metadata.nq(.gz) , merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz . Manifest & prepared queries: subgraph-manifest.json (partition registry) and queries.json (prepared SPARQL). Every file is sorted and de-duplicated, so unchanged partitions are byte-identical across rebuilds. Stage 2: Build-Time Tests bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts The test builds the dataset and checks: zero blank nodes; multi-condition search, date-range search and facet counts; additive community mounting; the discoverySearch prepared query; that the manifest's partition files exist; and that a rebuild over exported records leaves unchanged partitions byte-identical. Not yet checked by any test: every item declares a collection and community path; every bitstream declares bytes and media type; every item has a 10665/... Handle. Stage 3: CDN Distribution Exported data is published to Cloudflare : R2 behind the Cloudflare CDN, with release history in a git repository on Cloudflare Artifacts (see IRIS CDN Exporter: deployment ). scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts rebuilds the dataset over the exported records and lists each output file in the release manifest as graph/<file> : who-iris-spine.nq.gz (Tier 1 spine) subgraph-manifest.json (partition registry) iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq.gz (Tier 2 partitions) who-iris-dataset.nq.gz (merged graph) queries.json (prepared queries) The bytes are stored in R2 under sha256/<aa>/<digest> . Cache Policy: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on sha256/* . A changed file has a new digest, so a cached object never goes stale. Stage 4: Client-Side Execution (Browser WASM) The intended client pattern (no page in this repository loads Oxigraph yet; the replica's home page filters an index embedded in the page with plain JavaScript): Create an in-memory store: const store = new oxigraph.Store(); Fetch the spine ( who-iris-spine.nq.gz ) and subgraph-manifest.json . Decompress and load: store.load(decompressedNq, { format: 'application/n-quads' }) . Run prepared SPARQL locally for title search, year filters and open-access gates. When the user selects a community, fetch its .nq.gz partition from the manifest and store.load() it; existing quads are kept. 3. Formal Requirements (Checkable Specifications) ID Requirement Verification Method SR-1 No Binary Embeddings in Graph : No RDF literal or URI may represent raw file bytes (base64 or blob data). Bitstreams are nodes reached by dspace:hasBitstream , with fileName , fileBytes (integer) and mediaType . Not automated. SR-2 Upstream Skolemization at the Extractor (Zero Blank Nodes) : Extractors and ingestion pipelines assign deterministic URIs ( https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} ) at extraction for all compound nodes (creators, subjects, dates). No blank node ( _: ) may be emitted. The build throws on any residual blank node; iris-oxigraph.test.ts asserts none in the dataset. SR-3 Multi-Graph Isolation : Catalogue containment and rights gates reside in <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> ; bibliographic records in <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> . Not automated. The catalogue graph also carries rdf:type , rdfs:label and dcterms:title . SR-4 Sub-50ms Query Execution : Standard discovery and complex search queries over the materialized dataset complete in under 50 milliseconds in WASM. Not measured by any test. SR-5 Additive Subgraph Mounting : store.load() of an additional named subgraph must not clobber, mutate, or duplicate loaded quads. iris-oxigraph.test.ts : a query before mounting returns N items; after mounting a community, N + M. SR-6 Handle Authority : Every item subject URI uses the Handle system: https://hdl.handle.net/10665/{id} . Graph check: every a dspace:Item subject starts with https://hdl.handle.net/ . SR-7 Compressed Transport Ceiling : At full scale (300,000 items), a community partition must not exceed 25 MB compressed. Not measured in CI. SR-8 Prepared Query Equivalence : Every entry in queries.json is valid SPARQL 1.1 and runs against the dataset with 0 errors. iris-oxigraph.test.ts runs discoverySearch only. SR-9 Append-Only Streaming Partitioning : The build writes partitions as an append-only stream, with memory bounded regardless of corpus size (300,000 items). Not met: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is unused. Target: heap under 250 MB for the whole corpus. 4. Scale Modeling & Corpus Sizing (300,000 Items) WHO IRIS holds 273,559 items across 1,057,223 files , about 361.55 GiB of PDFs, reports and images (see iris-dspace §Scale). The figures below are estimates for about 300,000 items. Sizing Comparison: Raw Full-Text vs. Pure KG Extract in Oxigraph Metric Raw Full-Text in Oxigraph Pure KG Metadata Extract (Architecture Standard) Content Included Full OCR extracted page text + bibliographic metadata Dublin Core, MeSH authorities, bitstream descriptors, access gates, hierarchy paths Binary Blobs in RDF 0 (strictly excluded) 0 (strictly excluded) Quads / Triples ~45,000,000 quads (including sentence/paragraph chunks) ~12,000,000 quads (~40 quads per item) Uncompressed N-Quads ~45 – 60 GB ~1.2 – 1.5 GB Brotli / Gzip Payload ~8 – 12 GB compressed ~95 – 140 MB compressed (>90% compression ratio) Partition Size (per Community) ~1.2 – 1.8 GB compressed ~12 – 20 MB compressed WASM In-Memory RAM > 4 GB (Exceeds 32-bit WASM limit → Browser Crash ) ~35 – 65 MB RAM per loaded partition Load Time over CDN (4G/Fiber) Impossible in browser 150 ms – 350 ms Query Latency Slow regex/filter scans (> 5,000 ms) < 15 ms index-backed graph pattern matching Architectural Recommendation Never load full text into Oxigraph. Substring filters over millions of text literals are slow and exceed browser memory. Hybrid search: A static inverted index (e.g. Pagefind, MiniSearch, or a sharded SQLite FTS5 WASM slice) handles full-text lookup and yields candidate item IRIs. The candidates go into Oxigraph as VALUES ?item { ... } for facets, MeSH hierarchies, collection constraints and copyright gates. 5. Registered Tools, Skills & Verification Executable Scripts & Tools scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts : N-Quads compiler, skolemizer and gzip writer. scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts : IrisOxigraphEngine — boolean search, facet counts and incremental subgraph mounting. scripts/gen-iris-pages.ts : static site generator; the home page's facet chips and filters run over an index embedded in the page, not Oxigraph. Test Suites Unit: bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . End-to-end: bunx playwright test cat-harness-tools/test/who-iris-search.e2e.ts (browser search, facet chips, open-access filters, multilingual UI). Formal Skills & Specifications skills/iris-oxigraph.md : requirements OX-1 through OX-9 . docs/oxigraph-pipeline-requirements.md : system requirements SR-1 through SR-9 .

29e08be2401e.doc: Working on the WHO style guide's voices
29e08be2401e.title: Working on the WHO style guide's voices
29e08be2401e.content: What binds everywhere is who-iris's AGENTS.md , and through it the harness's; what the style guide is is style-guide.md . These rules govern the voices in skills/voices/ . A voice is DERIVED FROM a publication; it is not the publication The source documents live in this instance's library/ , and they stay there. Every rule in a voice cites { libraryId, sectionId } and resolves against that library. Do not copy source text into a voice. A rule carries its quote and its page so a reader can check it; a copied document is a second copy of a catalogued corpus, free to drift from it, with nothing to say which is authoritative. Every rule carries its quote and its page That is what makes a voice auditable. A rule without them is unsourced: a reader cannot tell whether it came from the publication or from an agent's impression of it. If you cannot find the page, mark the rule as un-located rather than dropping the citation: that is a different fact from a rule that never needed one. Adding a voice Derive it from one publication, read rule by rule. A voice assembled from several is a synthesis, not a house voice: a reader can no longer check a rule against the document it came from. Kept in docs/ rather than beside the voices because any .md other than a README inside a skills directory is read as a skill.

b4e1cc66f57f.title: The WHO style guide
b4e1cc66f57f.content: The WHO house voices and the WHO glossary : three editorial profiles, each read rule by rule out of one publication in this instance's library , with every rule carrying the quote and the page it came from. It is a subgraph of who-iris : part where graph typology the voices skills/voices/ voices , declared from within by skills/skills.json the glossary glossary/ glossary this page the who-iris-docs subgraph docs the rules for working on a voice style-guide-agents.md docs (not kept inside skills/ , where any non-README .md is read as a skill) The three voice read from rules who-editorial WHO Editorial Style Manual ( who-pub-tps-931 , 1993) spelling, capitalization, eponym form, reference layout, non-discriminatory language who-guideline-development Handbook for guideline development, 2nd ed ( 9789241548960-eng , 2014) how a recommendation is stated, graded and attributed who-publication-design WPRO publication style guide ( wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng , 2020) logo integrity, exclusion zone, brand colour, typeface, photo provenance Derived from the library A voice is derived from a publication; it is not the publication. So the voices sit beside the library and not inside it, and no source text is copied into them. Each source is cited in the bare { libraryId, sectionId } form, which resolves against the citing instance. The cross-instance form { instance, libraryId, sectionId } is supported for a voice whose source lives in another instance. A voice names its sources once, in sources[] , and each rule says which source it uses and where in that source, so a source's details are never written twice. Checking it bun run cat check:voices bun run cat check:glossary check:voices finds every instance with a voices/ directory and resolves each citation through the declaration of the instance that holds the source. It reports four kinds of failure separately, because each needs a different fix: unknown instance, no library graph, never ingested, and no such section.

b258f6fe817e.title: IRIS
b258f6fe817e.content: يتمثل الهدف الرئيسي للمستودع المؤسسي لتبادل المعلومات (IRIS) في إتاحة الوصول الرقمي المجاني إلى المنشورات العلمية والتقنية لمنظمة الصحة العالمية، بما في ذلك إسهامات مكاتبها القطرية ومكاتبها الإقليمية ومقرها الرئيسي. وإضافة إلى ذلك، يشمل IRIS الولايات التي حددتها الأجهزة الرئاسية للمنظمة بالتعاون مع الدول الأعضاء فيها. نسخة مستنسخة. لا شعار لمنظمة الصحة العالمية ولا صورة فوتوغرافية — ألوان فقط، مأخوذة من السمة iris-web المقيسة من صفحة الأنماط الخاصة بالموقع نفسه. ابحث في المواد المحفوظة بالقيمة وعددها 12 وفي المجتمعات والمجموعات المُحال إليها. وللعثور بالمعرّف على أي من العُقد المُحال إليها وعددها 223 ، ابحث هنا أو افتح البحث بالمعرّف . يُبلغ IRIS في المصدر الأصلي عن 273,559 مادة موزعة على 1,057,223 ملفًا. أحدث التقديمات مرتبة حسب dc.date.accessioned ، الأحدث أولًا — وهو المفتاح الذي يرتّب به IRIS قائمته. وحين يحمل السجل عدة تواريخ إيداع يُستخدم أحدثها؛ ولمادة المكتب الإقليمي لغرب المحيط الهادئ (WPRO) تاريخان، بينهما خمسة أيام، والثاني هو تاريخ الدمج مع IRIS الإقليمي. Stratégie régionale pour améliorer l'accès aux médicaments et aux vaccins dans la Méditerranée orientale, pour la période 2020-2030 : accélérer la mise en oeuvre grâce à des systèmes de réglementation plus solides Organisation mondiale de la Santé. Bureau régional de la Méditerranée orientale (تاريخ النشر: 2026-09-15 ) لا يوجد dc.description.abstract في السجل الملتقط. غير محفوظ هنا Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery World Health Organization (تاريخ النشر: 2026-07-22 ) HIV remains a major public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective treatment and prevention tools. Many evidence-based interventions are not implemented consistently or delivered in a timely manner, contributing to ongoing HIV transmission, advanced disease and preventable mortality. These consolidated WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to strengthen HIV service delivery through people-centred, integrated and equitable approaches that improve access to care, continuity of treatment and accelerate progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat. The publication consolidates all WHO recommendations on HIV service delivery issued between 2013 and 2025. It is intended to support the development of national and subnational policies, clinical guidelines and implementation guidance. It addresses key components of HIV service delivery, including linkage to care and antiretroviral therapy initiation, clinical follow-up and medication refills, adherence support and re-engagement in care, services for adolescents and young people, task sharing, decentralized service delivery, and integration with maternal and child health, tuberculosis, sexual and reproductive health, diabetes, hypertension and mental health services. Recommendations are classified as new, updated or revalidated according to WHO guideline development procedures. غير محفوظ هنا National health workforce accounts: health workforce levels and trends 2026 World Health Organization (تاريخ النشر: 2026-06-22 ) This report presents the 2026 edition of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) series, providing an overview of the status of NHWA implementation and an analysis of global and regional health workforce levels and trends based on official data reported by countries to the World Health Organization. Developed to support evidence-informed health workforce policy-making and planning, the report examines progress in strengthening national health workforce information systems, data availability and reporting across countries, and the use of standardized indicators to monitor human resources for health in support of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other health objectives. Drawing on the 2025 NHWA data release, the report analyses the distribution, density and composition of the health and care workforce across regions and income groups, highlighting persistent disparities in workforce availability. It also examines trends in workforce growth since 2006 and presents a thematic analysis of population ageing and health workforce ageing, assessing their implications for future workforce needs.
